claims.assertion: The GPS track shows one off-route segment on this RydeTAXI trip: 12:12–12:16, where 2.93 km were driven over ground the optimal route covers in 0.80 km, adding 2.13 km and straying up to 954 m from the optimal route (F3); overall the trip ran 10.7 km against an optimal 8.4 km, +2.3 km (+27%) (F1).

No exemption applies to that segment: there were no in-app messages at all (F7), so the rider gave no consent of any kind before the segment started, and the driver's post-trip statement that 'the GPS rerouted' me is a claim, not rider consent, and verbal agreement asserted only by the driver does not count (F8).

The driver's congestion justification fails on the only evidence RD-4 accepts: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F11), the only speed records are band 4 (30–39 km/h) on the AYE and band 5 (40–49 km/h) on Jurong Town Hall Road (F9, F10) — neither is band 1 or 2 — and weather was fair with 0.0 mm rain (F12). The off-route segment is therefore unexempted.

RydeTAXI is a metered service, so the extra 2.13 km of the unexempted segment went straight into the meter; the fare billed distance of $15.14 over 10.74 km gives this trip's per-km rate of $1.4097, so the refundable mileage is 2.13 km × $1.4097 = $3.00 (fare fact F4 already computes the parallel figure: 2.31 km × $1.4097/km = $3.26).
No add-on was charged for the stopped/slow portion: waiting fee is $0.00 and there is no surge (F6, F5), so nothing further is claimed beyond the mileage of the unexempted segment.

The driver has 2 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days (F14), against the rider's clean record of 0 upheld disputes (F13); as this case establishes a fresh RD-1 breach, the account flag is warranted as a rider-side ancillary request only, and the finding stands on the GPS and fare records regardless of the profile.

weaknesses: F4 is the fare record and it frames the excess as 2.31 km × $1.4097 = $3.26, whereas the segment arithmetic in F3 gives 2.13 km; the driver will argue the higher, fare-derived excess and the judge may reasonably award $3.26 instead of the $3.00 I compute, since RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra_km and not every excess kilometre between route corridor 200 m wobble or mismatched length.

The rider's own 90-day record (F13) shows 1 dispute with 0 upheld, which the driver may use to suggest the rider is a habitual complainer; it is weak because an unupheld dispute is still a dispute and it does not touch the GPS excess in F3.

The optimal-route baseline of 8.4 km comes from the app estimate quoted in the complaint and echoed by F1/F2; the driver could contest that the app estimate is not the legally shortest route and ask for a route-by-route reconstruction, which the fact table does not contain (G13-type gap) — but F3's off-route segment measurement up to 954 m from the optimal route is a system record and survives that attack.

The driver's 'the GPS rerouted me' statement (F8) is uncorroborated by any traffic incident (F11) and would fail RD-4, but if the court treated a GPS unit's own rerouting as a reasonable cause, the segment could be exempted and the refund would drop to $0 — no fact in the table supports that reading, which is why I rely on F11 and F9/F10.

claims.assertion: The trip was a RydeTAXI metered run: the $24.80 charged is composed of base $3.90, distance $15.14 for 10.74 km, time $4.29 for 16.5 min and platform $1.47, with no waiting fee and no surge (F5, F6), so the complaint is a metered-mileage dispute, not a fixed-quote dispute.

The GPS record shows one continuous off-route segment, 12:12–12:16, driving 2.93 km where the optimal route covers 0.80 km and adding 2.13 km (F3), with the whole trip 10.7 km against an 8.4 km optimal route (F1) — that single segment is the only deviation the driver must explain.

The driver's account that he simply followed a GPS reroute (F8) is a bare statement contradicted by the system record, which shows a detour reaching 954 m off the optimal corridor (F3) and no traffic incident on the route (F11); on the record there is no justification for the segment.

There is no consent defence: the chat record contains no in-app messages at all (F7) and the driver's written statement mentions no rider instruction (F8), so no message from the rider precedes the 12:12 segment start; consent cannot rest on the driver's after-the-fact account.

No traffic exemption is available: no traffic incident was recorded near the route during the trip window (F11); the only band records are Ayer Rajah Expressway at band 4 (30–39 km/h) and Jurong Town Hall Road at band 5 (40–49 km/h) (F9, F10), neither of which is band 1 or 2 and neither of which is tied to the replaced stretch of the optimal route, and conditions were fair with 0.0 mm rain (F12).

The excess distance attributable to the detour was billed at $3.26 (2.31 km × $1.4097/km, the trip's distance fare divided by distance km) (F4, F6), so the maximum distance-based refund on the strict RD-2 basis is one of $3.26 (all billed excess) or $3.00 (the 2.13 km actually added by the single segment, F3) — the driver asks the court to apply the narrower segment-only measure of $3.00 rather than the full billed excess.
The extra $4.29 time component (16.5 min actual vs 13.8 min estimated; F2, F6) is a meter time unit charge and is not refundable under RD-2, which refunds distance units only.

The driver has 378 days of account history, a 4.63 rating over 963 trips in 90 days (F14), which supports a proportionate outcome and an argument against account action; the two prior upheld route disputes in 90 days (F14) are noted but the 90-day picture is not one of a driver with a repeated pattern of this case's single segment.

weaknesses: The system record is against us on the central facts: F3 shows a single off-route segment adding 2.13 km and reaching 954 m off the optimal route, and F1 shows +2.3 km (+27%) overall, so the RD-1 breach cannot realistically be denied — the argument is only about amount and about the driver's account in F8 not being corroborated by F11/F9/F10.

The driver's written statement in F8 ("I went where the GPS sent me; it rerouted") has no supporting record: F11 shows no traffic incident and F9/F10 show only band 4/5 speeds, so the rider will use F8 together with F11 as proof the reroute was unexplained under RD-4.

The absence of any chat at all (F7) removes every route-consent argument under RD-5; the rider will say there was no warning whatsoever before the 12:12–12:16 segment, and we cannot point to any message that preceded the segment start.

F14 shows 2 upheld route disputes in the last 90 days, and RP-6's condition (upheld_90d ≥ 1 plus a refund > 0 here) is met on its face, so the rider may obtain a flag_account rider-side request that we can only resist on proportionality grounds, not on the facts.

points.response: Accepted: F5 and F6 confirm this is a RydeTAXI metered run with no surge and no waiting fee, which is exactly the basis on which RD-2 gives the rider a mileage refund rather than a fixed-quote argument — the metered structure is what makes the extra 2.13 km (F3) chargeable-plus-refundable.

Agreed on the record: F3 identifies the single off-route segment 12:12–12:16 driving 2.93 km where the optimal route covers 0.80 km (+2.13 km, up to 954 m off), and F1 shows 10.7 km against 8.4 km optimal (+27%) — that one unexempted segment is the whole rider claim.

The driver's own advocate concedes the F8 'GPS rerouted me' account is bare; the system record F3 (954 m off the optimal corridor) plus the absence of any incident in F11 leaves the segment unexplained and unexempted under RD-4(c).
Conceded: with no in-app messages at all (F7) there is no rider message before the 12:12 segment start, and RD-5 / G11 bar resting consent on the driver's after-the-fact statement in F8.

Agreed, and this is the rider's strongest point: F11 records no incident, F9/F10 record only band 4 and band 5 speeds rather than band 1/2, and F12 shows fair weather, so RD-4(a) is not met and RD-4(b) cannot exempt the segment on its own.

The rider accepts the narrower measure and keeps the request at $3.00, computed as the segment's own 2.13 km (F3) at this trip's per-km rate of $1.4097 derived from the distance fare $15.14 ÷ 10.74 km (F4, F6), because RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's extra_km and not the residual excess the fare record lumps in as 2.31 km × $1.4097 = $3.26 (F4).
Conceded: RD-2 refunds mileage units only, so the $4.29 time component (16.5 min vs 13.8 min estimated; F2, F6) is not part of the rider's claim.

The driver's 378-day, 4.63-rating, 963-trip history (F14) goes to proportionality of the refund but not to the RD-6 flag: the same F14 records 2 route disputes upheld in the last 90 days, so once this case establishes a fresh RD-1 breach with a refund above zero, RD-6's condition is met and the account-review request stands.

Conceded as to the finding: F3 records the single off-route segment (12:12–12:16, +2.13 km, up to 954 m off the optimal route) and F1 the +2.3 km overall, so RD-1 is breached on that one segment and the driver does not contest it.

Accepted: F7 shows no in-app messages at all and F8 is the driver's own post-trip statement, so there is no pre-segment rider consent under RD-5 and the driver does not rely on 'the GPS rerouted me' as consent.
Conceded: F11 records no traffic incident near the route, F9/F10 are only band 4 and band 5 (neither band 1 nor 2), and F12 shows fair weather, so no RD-4 exemption attaches to the segment.

Agreed in substance but on the narrower measure: RD-2 refunds only the unexempted segment's own extra_km, and F3 fixes that at 2.13 km, so the refund should be the segment figure rather than the whole $3.26 billed excess in F4; the driver nonetheless accepts $3.00 as the practical outcome and the rider's own arithmetic matches it.
Agreed: F6 shows waiting $0.00 and F5 shows no surge, so nothing beyond the unexempted segment's mileage is in dispute.

The profile cannot decide anything and must not drive the finding: F14's two upheld route disputes concern past 90-day history while F13 shows the rider's own 90-day record is 1 dispute, 0 upheld, and RD-6 attach is discretionary account review, so the driver asks the court to record the breach and the $3.00 refund without adding an account flag on profile evidence alone.

notices.text: We reviewed your trip and found one part of the route went off course: about 2.13 km driven on roads the direct route doesn't cover. Nothing in your messages agreed to that detour, and there was no traffic incident or bad weather to explain it. So we're giving you $3.00 back, as a Ryde voucher added to your account. The rest of the fare stands, including the time charge. Your driver's account is also being referred for review because this kind of route issue has come up before.

We reviewed this trip's route record. One stretch of about 2.13 km took you off the direct route with no rider agreement to it, and no recorded traffic incident or weather problem explains it. The outcome is a $3.00 voucher refund to the rider, based on this trip's per-km rate. Separately, your account is being referred for review, since your recent record shows more than one upheld routing dispute. No other action on this trip.
